title: “I KNOW THAT MY REDEEMER LIVES” — BUT WHAT IF JOB WAS SAYING SOMETHING FAR MORE DESPERATE THAN WE EVER REALIZED?
paragraphs: “I KNOW THAT MY REDEEMER LIVES” — BUT WHAT IF JOB WAS SAYING SOMETHING FAR MORE DESPERATE THAN WE EVER REALIZED?

He had buried his children, lost everything he owned, and watched his body fall apart. Then, from the ashes of a life that no longer made sense, Job spoke words that would echo across thousands of years. But what did he actually mean? The answer is more painful, more complicated, and ultimately more beautiful than the familiar verse on our walls.
There are words you can only understand after life has broken your heart.
Words that sound beautiful when sung in church but become almost impossible to whisper when you're sitting alone in a hospital corridor, waiting for news you don't want to hear.
Words that feel powerful when everything is going well but seem to disappear when the person you prayed for dies anyway.
And then there are five words that have survived centuries of suffering.
“I know that my redeemer liveth.”
Job 19:25, King James Version.
We have embroidered those words onto pillows. Printed them on bookmarks. Sung them at Easter. Spoken them at funerals.
But have we ever stopped long enough to ask what was happening to the man who first said them?
Because Job wasn't standing in a beautiful sanctuary when he made that declaration.
He wasn't celebrating a miracle.
His circumstances hadn't improved.
His children were still dead.
His wealth was still gone.
His skin was still diseased.
His friends were still accusing him.
And God had not yet explained anything.
Job was sitting in the wreckage of a life he could no longer recognize.
And somehow, from that place, he said something extraordinary.
Not because he understood what God was doing.
But because he desperately needed someone who could stand for him when nobody else would.
And perhaps that is where this story begins to become yours.
Maybe you've never lost everything Job lost.
But you know what it feels like to pray until your voice grows tired.
You know what it's like to smile at people who have no idea how close you are to falling apart.
You know the strange loneliness of believing in God while quietly wondering why He seems so far away.
And maybe you've heard this verse a hundred times without realizing that the man who spoke it was not delivering a polished sermon about victory.
He was fighting to keep his case, his dignity, and his hope alive.
To understand why, we have to go back to the ashes.
Job's suffering began with a devastating series of losses.

According to Job 1, messengers arrived one after another with increasingly terrible news. His livestock were stolen or destroyed. His servants were killed. Then came the message no parent should ever have to receive.
His sons and daughters had died when a great wind struck the house where they were gathered.
Seven sons.
Three daughters.
Gone.
In a matter of moments, the future he had imagined disappeared.
Then, in Job 2, his own body became a place of suffering. Painful sores covered him, and he sat among ashes, scraping himself with a broken piece of pottery.
The man who had once been respected was now a spectacle of misery.
And what makes the story especially disturbing is that the opening chapters describe Job as upright and God-fearing.
His suffering was not presented as punishment for some hidden wickedness.
The reader is allowed to see a heavenly conversation that Job himself never hears.
Job doesn't know why these things are happening.
He only knows they are happening.
And that distinction matters.
Because some of the deepest spiritual wounds come not merely from suffering, but from suffering without an explanation.
When the diagnosis comes despite the prayers.
When the marriage collapses despite the promises.
When the child walks away despite years of teaching and tears.
When you search your conscience and cannot find the terrible crime that supposedly explains your terrible pain.
Then people begin offering answers.
Perhaps you didn't pray enough.
Perhaps your faith was weak.
Perhaps God is exposing something.
Perhaps you brought this upon yourself.
Job knew what it meant to be wounded by people who thought they understood his suffering better than he did.
His friends initially came to comfort him, and their first response was remarkable. They sat with him in silence for seven days and seven nights because his suffering was so great (Job 2:13).
But eventually, silence gave way to speeches.
And their explanations became another burden.
They repeatedly appealed to the idea that God rewards the righteous and punishes the wicked, implying that Job's catastrophe must reveal something wrong in him.
They were defending a tidy explanation of the world.
Job was living in a world that no longer fit their explanation.
By chapter 19, his anguish had become almost unbearable.
He cried out:
“How long will ye vex my soul, and break me in pieces with words?”
Job 19:2, KJV.
Read that again.
“Break me in pieces with words.”
Some people know exactly what that feels like.
You survived the crisis, but almost didn't survive what people said about it.
You endured the betrayal, only to hear someone question your character.
You carried grief, only to be told you should have moved on.
You confessed that you were struggling, and someone used your honesty as evidence against you.
Job's friends were speaking about righteousness while failing to show compassion to the righteous sufferer sitting in front of them.
And Job was painfully aware of it.
He described feeling abandoned by relatives, acquaintances, servants, and close companions. He believed that even those who once loved him had turned against him (Job 19:13–19).
Then came one of the most heartbreaking appeals in the entire book:
“Have pity upon me, have pity upon me, O ye my friends; for the hand of God hath touched me.”
Job 19:21, KJV.
This was not the voice of a man pretending to be strong.
This was a wounded human being begging for mercy.
And immediately afterward, something unexpected happened.
Job began speaking as though he wanted his words preserved forever.
“Oh that my words were now written! oh that they were printed in a book!”
Job 19:23, KJV.
He wanted his testimony recorded.
He wanted it engraved where it could not easily be erased.
Why?
Because everyone around him seemed convinced that his suffering proved his guilt.
He wanted the truth of his case to survive him.
And then came the declaration.
“For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth.”
Job 19:25, KJV.
This is where we need to be careful.
Because the English word redeemer is beautiful, but the original Hebrew carries a depth that can easily be missed.
The Hebrew text begins:
וַאֲנִי יָדַעְתִּי גֹּאֲלִי חָי
Va'ani yada'ti go'ali chai.
A close translation is:
“But I, I know that my redeemer lives.”
Notice the force of the opening.
Va'ani — “But I” or “As for me.”
It stands in contrast to the voices surrounding him.
His friends have their accusations.
His circumstances appear to testify against him.
His own body is deteriorating.
But Job insists that there is something he knows, even amid everything he cannot understand.
Then comes the crucial word.
גֹּאֲלִי — go'ali.
“My go'el.”
The Hebrew term go'el refers to a redeemer or vindicator, often someone with a recognized responsibility to act on behalf of a family member.
In ancient Israel, a go'el could be involved in recovering family property, protecting family interests, or carrying out certain obligations of kinship and justice.
Leviticus 25:25 describes a close relative redeeming property that an impoverished family member had sold.
Ruth 4 presents Boaz acting within the institution of family redemption, although the legal circumstances there are more complex than simply rescuing someone from trouble.
Numbers 35 also uses related terminology for the avenger of blood.
The central idea is not merely that someone feels sympathy.
It is that someone has the standing and responsibility to act.
Someone who will not let a person's claim simply disappear.
Someone who can intervene when the vulnerable have no power to defend themselves.
Now return to Job.
His relatives have withdrawn.
His friends have turned into accusers.
His reputation has been shattered.
He feels abandoned by everyone who should have stood beside him.
And suddenly he declares that his go'el lives.
Do you see the emotional weight?
Job is not merely saying, “I believe things will eventually get better.”
He is reaching for the hope that there is a living vindicator who can speak for him when the world has already pronounced its verdict.
He wants someone to establish the truth.
Someone who will not mistake his suffering for proof of wickedness.
Someone who will stand when everyone else has walked away.
But who exactly is this redeemer?
Here we must resist the temptation to give a simple answer where the text itself invites careful interpretation.
Throughout the book, Job longs for someone who can mediate between himself and God.
In Job 9:33, he laments the absence of an arbiter who could lay a hand upon both parties.
In Job 16:19, he says:
“Also now, behold, my witness is in heaven, and my record is on high.”
KJV.
Job appears to be reaching toward heavenly testimony, vindication, and justice.
Many interpreters understand the redeemer in Job 19 as a heavenly advocate, ultimately associated with God Himself.
Others understand the passage differently, and scholars continue to debate the precise identity of the go'el, the timing of his appearance, and whether Job expects vindication before or after death.
That debate is not a weakness in Scripture.
It is a reminder that faithfulness to Scripture sometimes requires admitting where the ancient wording is difficult.
And the next words are especially difficult.
The Hebrew of Job 19:25 continues:
וְאַחֲרוֹן עַל־עָפָר יָקוּם
Ve'acharon al-'afar yaqum.
The wording can be understood along the lines of:
“And at the last he will stand upon the dust.”
The Hebrew word 'afar means dust or loose earth.
The King James Version renders the phrase “at the latter day upon the earth,” a familiar and deeply influential translation.
But the Hebrew does not explicitly contain a separate word meaning “day” in that phrase.
Nor does the verse, by itself, clearly describe every detail of a final resurrection or Christ's second coming.
Those are theological questions that require attention to the wider biblical revelation.
The language of standing upon the dust may suggest a final act of vindication in the face of human mortality.
It may evoke the earth itself, the dust from which human beings come and to which they return.
It may even carry courtroom-like implications of someone rising to establish a case.
The precise imagery remains disputed.
But the emotional force is unmistakable.
Job believes that death, decay, and accusation will not necessarily have the final word.
Then comes Job 19:26–27, one of the most discussed passages in the entire Old Testament.
The KJV reads:
“And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God:
Whom I shall see for myself, and mine eyes shall behold, and not another; though my reins be consumed within me.”
There is something breathtaking about those words.
Job longs to see God.
Not merely to hear about Him from people who claim to understand His ways.
Not merely to receive another explanation from a friend.
He wants an encounter with the One who knows the truth.
But the Hebrew text is unusually difficult here.
The wording translated “in my flesh” can also be understood as “from my flesh” or, in some interpretations, “apart from my flesh.”
That difference matters.
One reading points toward seeing God bodily.
Another may suggest seeing God beyond the destruction of the body.
Some interpreters see in these verses an anticipation of resurrection. Others understand Job as expecting a vindication or vision of God without a clearly developed doctrine of bodily resurrection.
The passage does not allow us to settle every question with absolute certainty.
And we should not pretend that it does.
But there is something we can say with confidence: Job's hope is not rooted in the recovery of his possessions. It is rooted in the possibility that he will finally be vindicated before God.
That changes how we hear the verse.
Job's deepest longing is not simply for a new house, new livestock, or the return of his former social standing.
He wants the truth to be known.
He wants God.
And that longing is painfully relevant to anyone who has ever whispered:
“Lord, I don't even need everyone to understand me anymore. I just need You to know.”
Perhaps you are there right now.
Perhaps your name has been dragged through conversations you were never invited into.
Perhaps you've been blamed for a family conflict you tried desperately to prevent.
Perhaps you have spent years carrying a grief nobody sees.
Or perhaps your greatest accusation is not coming from another person.
Perhaps it comes from your own conscience.
You remember what you did.
The lie.
The betrayal.
The secret.
The compromise you promised would never happen again.
You wonder whether someone like you can still approach a holy God.
Job's situation and yours may be very different. The book insists on Job's integrity against the accusations of his friends, while some of us must honestly acknowledge real sins.
But both situations bring us face-to-face with a question that reaches beyond human ability.
Who can stand for us before God?
And here the Christian story leads us to Jesus Christ.
We must distinguish what Job could have understood in his historical setting from what Christians can see when reading his words in the light of the New Testament.
Job did not possess the completed New Testament.
We should not claim that he consciously knew every detail of Jesus' incarnation, crucifixion, and resurrection.
Nor should we force every uncertain Hebrew phrase into a prediction more specific than the text itself establishes.
But the whole biblical story gives Christian readers a remarkable reason to hear Job's longing with renewed hope.
Job cried out for a mediator.
The New Testament announces:
“For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.”
1 Timothy 2:5, KJV.
Job longed for a living vindicator.
The New Testament declares that Jesus Christ died, rose again, and intercedes for His people.
Romans 8:34 says:
“Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us.”
KJV.
Job wanted someone who could stand when human voices condemned him.
The Gospel announces a Savior who has borne sin, defeated death, and opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
This is not because Job 19 contains every detail of the Gospel in advance.
It is because the Gospel provides the fullest Christian answer to the human longing for redemption, mediation, justice, and life beyond death.
And the difference between Job's longing and Christ's finished work is astonishing.
Job needed someone to establish his innocence against false accusations.
We need something even greater.
We need someone who can deal with the accusations that are true.
Because there are things we cannot honestly deny.
We have sinned.
We have failed.
We have loved lesser things more than God.
We have wounded others and justified ourselves.
We have made promises to God and broken them.
And no amount of religious performance can rewrite what has already happened.
But listen carefully.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to defend people who have never done anything wrong.
He came to save sinners.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
KJV.
While we were still sinners.
Not after we had repaired our reputations.
Not after we had learned to sound spiritual.
Not after we had finally become the people we pretended to be.
While we were still sinners.
This is the scandal of grace.
The Holy One willingly gave Himself for the unholy.
The innocent Christ suffered for the guilty.
The Son of God entered a world filled with betrayal, injustice, suffering, and death, and through His cross accomplished the redemption we could never earn.
And He did not remain in the grave.
The apostle Paul wrote:
“But now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept.”
1 Corinthians 15:20, KJV.
That resurrection changes everything.
Not because Christians are promised a painless life.
Not because every faithful person receives a miracle on demand.
Not because every earthly injustice is immediately corrected.
But because the crucified and risen Jesus has defeated death and secured a future that suffering cannot finally destroy.
When Jesus told Martha, whose brother Lazarus had died, “I am the resurrection, and the life,” He was not offering a motivational slogan.
He was identifying Himself as the source of life and resurrection hope.
John 11:25.
And when He stood outside Lazarus's tomb, Jesus wept.
John 11:35.
Consider that.
The One who knew He would raise Lazarus still entered the grief of those who mourned.
He did not treat their tears as a theological embarrassment.
He did not shame them for grieving.
He wept.
Somebody reading this needs to know that Christian hope does not require you to stop being human.
You can believe in the resurrection and still cry at a graveside.
You can trust God's promises and still feel frightened before surgery.
You can love Jesus and still ask why the road has become so painful.
You can worship with tears.
Faith is not the absence of sorrow.
And sorrow is not proof that faith has died.
Job himself refused to hide his anguish behind religious language.
He lamented.
He protested.
He questioned.
At times, his words were so fierce that they make modern believers uncomfortable.
And yet God did not ultimately endorse the simplistic accusations of Job's friends.
In Job 42:7, the Lord rebuked them for not speaking rightly about Him as Job had.
That does not mean every statement Job made was beyond correction. God confronted Job's limited understanding in chapters 38–41, and Job responded with humility.
But the book refuses to equate honest suffering with hidden wickedness.
That should change the way we treat hurting people.
Not every hospital bed is the consequence of a secret sin.
Not every financial collapse is evidence of divine rejection.
Not every broken marriage can be explained by one person's lack of faith.
Not every unanswered prayer means God has stopped listening.
Jesus Himself challenged the assumption that suffering always reveals unusually great personal guilt (Luke 13:1–5; John 9:1–3).
Sometimes the most Christlike thing you can do is stop explaining someone's pain and begin carrying it with them.
Sit beside them.
Bring food.
Pray without performing.
Listen without correcting every tear.
And when words finally become necessary, speak with the gentleness of someone who remembers that grace was given to you before you could ever deserve it.
There is another detail in Job's story that we cannot afford to miss.
When God finally speaks from the whirlwind, He does not hand Job a complete explanation of the heavenly events described in the opening chapters.
Instead, God reveals His wisdom, power, and the vastness of a creation Job cannot fully comprehend.
Job receives an encounter, not the detailed answer he had demanded.
And in Job 42:5, he says:
“I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee.”
KJV.
There is an extraordinary connection here.
Earlier, Job had longed to see God for himself.
At the end, he speaks of having encountered God in a way that transformed his understanding.
This is not the same as saying every question was resolved.
Nor is it the final resurrection described in the New Testament.
But within Job's story, the encounter with God becomes more decisive than the explanations offered by human beings.
Job learns that he is not in control of the universe.
He also learns that his suffering cannot be reduced to the neat moral arithmetic of his friends.
And eventually, his fortunes are restored.
But please don't rush through that ending.
Job 42 records renewed prosperity and the birth of more children.
It does not say that his earlier children never mattered.
It does not say that the grief of losing them simply vanished.
Children are not replaceable possessions.
A later blessing does not erase the reality of an earlier wound.
The book ends with restoration, but it never invites us to pretend that Job's suffering was imaginary.
And this matters because some of us have been waiting for God to restore something that will never return in exactly the same form.
A loved one who has died.
A childhood that was stolen.
Years lost to addiction.
A relationship destroyed by betrayal.
An opportunity that passed.
A version of life that no longer exists.
The Christian hope is not that God will rewind every event until nothing painful ever happened.
Our hope is that through Jesus Christ, evil, sin, suffering, and death will not have the ultimate victory.
Revelation 21:4 promises a future in which God will wipe away every tear, and death, sorrow, crying, and pain will be no more.
That promise reaches further than temporary relief.
It points toward the renewal of all things under the reign of God.
And it is grounded in the victory of the risen Christ.
So when Christians say, “I know that my Redeemer lives,” we can say it with a confidence Job could only reach toward from within his ancient suffering.
We know the name of the One in whom our redemption is fulfilled.
Jesus Christ.
We know that He was crucified.
We know that the apostolic Gospel proclaims His bodily resurrection.
We know that salvation is offered by grace through faith, not purchased by our works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
We know that repentance and forgiveness of sins are proclaimed in His name (Luke 24:46–47).
And we know that His resurrection is the foundation of our own future resurrection hope (1 Corinthians 15).
But knowing these truths does not mean we will always feel strong.
There will still be nights when the room is silent and the heart is loud.
There will still be prayers that seem to rise no higher than the ceiling.
There will still be days when you read Scripture and feel nothing.
There will still be people who misunderstand you.
And there may be moments when all you can offer God is a broken sentence.
“Lord, I still believe. Help my unbelief.”
That is not a polished declaration.
It is the kind of prayer a desperate father brought to Jesus in Mark 9:24.
And Jesus did not require him to manufacture perfect emotional certainty before bringing his need.
Maybe your faith feels like that today.
Small.
Bruised.
Exhausted.
Still reaching.
Then hear this.
The strength of your Savior is not measured by the intensity of your feelings.
Christ does not cease to live when you struggle to feel His presence.
His resurrection does not become less true because your eyes are filled with tears.
And His grace does not become unavailable because you finally admit how desperately you need it.
But grace is not permission to remain comfortable in sin.
The same Jesus who welcomes sinners calls them to repentance.
He does not merely cover our shame so we can continue living as though nothing matters.
He forgives, cleanses, and transforms.
He calls us out of darkness and into His light.
He teaches us to confess what we have hidden, abandon what is destroying us, forgive where we have been wounded, and follow Him even when obedience is costly.
And when we fall, we do not have to run deeper into hiding.
First John 1:9 reminds believers that God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse those who confess their sins.
That is the beauty of redemption.
Jesus does not simply offer a better public image.
He offers reconciliation with God.
Not a cosmetic improvement.
A new life.
Not the erasure of every earthly consequence.
But the forgiveness, hope, and transformation that flow from His saving work.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by turning suffering into entertainment.
But by accomplishing a redemption so profound that the worst chapter of a person's life does not have to become the final definition of that person.
The cross proves that sin is serious.
The resurrection proves that death is defeated.
And the Gospel announces that sinners can come home.
Maybe the scandal in your story is something someone did to you.
Maybe it is something you did.
Maybe it is a private battle nobody knows about.
Maybe it is the painful collapse of the life you thought God was going to give you.
Whatever it is, you do not have to pretend that it is beautiful.
Bring the truth into the light.
Bring your grief.
Bring your confession.
Bring your questions.
Bring the exhausted faith that can barely form a prayer.
And come to Christ.
Not because you have earned an audience with Him.
But because the Gospel declares that through Him we may draw near to God.
There is a reason Hebrews 7:25 is so precious:
“Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them.”
KJV.
He ever lives.
Job said, “My redeemer lives.”
The New Testament declares that the risen Christ continues as the living intercessor for those who come to God through Him.
What Job longed for in the midst of accusation, Christians find their ultimate answer to in Jesus.
And this is why the words matter so deeply.
Because the most important question is not whether everyone on earth will eventually understand your story.
It is whether you have come to the Savior who can reconcile you to God.
Your friends may misunderstand.
Your enemies may accuse.
Your past may be impossible to change.
Your body may weaken.
Your possessions may disappear.
And one day, unless Christ returns first, earthly life itself will end.
But the risen Jesus remains alive.
That is not an escape from reality.
It is the foundation of Christian hope in the face of reality.
What is the part of your life where you most desperately need to remember that your Redeemer lives?
Is it grief?
Is it guilt?
Is it a secret battle?
Is it the fear that God has forgotten you?
Is it the exhaustion of trying to remain faithful while everything around you seems to be falling apart?
You do not have to tell strangers the details of a wound you are not ready to share.
If you have been fighting quietly and need someone to stand with you in prayer, you are welcome here.
Don't underestimate what a sincere testimony can do for a person who feels alone.
And don't underestimate what happens when Scripture reaches someone at exactly the moment they are tempted to give up.
Not to expose their struggles.
Not to embarrass them.
But to remind them that they have not been forgotten.

We want this community to be a place where Scripture is taken seriously, where difficult questions are not ignored, where grace is never separated from truth, and where people are continually pointed toward Jesus Christ.
And if you have been strengthened by this ministry and want to help its work continue, I want to extend a personal invitation.
And not because financial support is the measure of your faith.
It isn't.
The Gospel is free, and the grace of God cannot be bought.

But Scripture does encourage willing, generous support for faithful Gospel ministry. Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver. Galatians 6:6 speaks of sharing good things with those who teach the Word, and Philippians 4:15–18 records believers participating financially in Paul's ministry.
It can be part of your personal generosity to God, alongside your responsibilities to your local church, your household, and others in need.
It should not be treated as a required biblical tithe, a replacement for every other form of Christian giving, or a guarantee of blessing.
What matters is a willing heart, faithful stewardship, and a desire to see Christ honored.
Those resources are part of our desire to nourish faith, encourage spiritual maturity, and help people return to the Word of God again and again.
Pray for the ministry.
Encourage someone who is struggling.
Keep reading the Scriptures.
Keep testing every teaching against the Word of God.
Keep pointing people to Jesus rather than to a personality, a page, or a platform.
Because Gospel Warrior is not the Redeemer.
Jesus is.
Jesus saves.
A library cannot forgive sins.
Jesus forgives.
A community cannot conquer death.
Jesus Christ has risen.

And that is the message worth carrying into every home, every broken family, every hospital room, every prison cell, every exhausted heart, and every corner of the world where someone has begun to believe that hope is gone.
Perhaps that is why Job's ancient words have endured.
Not because they offer a simple explanation for every tragedy.
Not because they promise that suffering will end tomorrow.
Not because Job had already seen everything Christians now know about the risen Savior.
But because they give voice to something that suffering cannot easily silence.
The longing for a living Redeemer.
A vindicator.
Someone who will stand.
Someone whose life is not extinguished by the grave.
And in Jesus Christ, the Christian faith proclaims that redemption is no longer merely a longing reaching into the darkness.
The Redeemer has come.
He has suffered.
He has died.
He has risen.
And He lives forever.
So tonight, if your heart is heavy, you do not have to pretend everything is okay.
If you need to repent, repent.
If you need to confess, confess.
If you need to grieve, grieve.
If you need help, ask for it.
If you need to pray through tears, pray through tears.
But do not mistake the darkness of your circumstances for the death of your Savior.
Job's world fell apart, but his longing for a living Redeemer remained.
And for those who belong to Jesus Christ, the resurrection gives that hope its surest foundation.
The ashes may still be beneath your feet, but the tomb of your Redeemer is empty.
